newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian foreign minister warns of U.S. sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Colombian foreign minister warns of U.S. sanctions.

text.p: Foreign Minister Maria Emma Mejia said on Tuesday that Colombia would probably be hit with economic sanctions if two draft laws tightening penalties for drug trafficking failed to pass in Congress.
"If these laws are not approved it would be a clear sign of the country's lack of will to fight drug trafficking seriously," Mejia told reporters.
She added a terse "sure" when asked if Washington could be expected to impose economic sanctions on Colombia if its lawmakers declined to approve the anti-drug legislation.

The legislation would establish stiffer prison sentences for drug traffickers and give the government sweeping powers to confiscate the assets of convicted drug lords and those who conspire with them.

Mejia spoke after closed-door talks early on Tuesday with U.S. Ambassador Myles Frechette. Justice Minister Carlos Medellin and chief prosecutor Alfonso Valdivieso were also present at the talks, which were widely believed to focus on the fate of the anti-drug laws that have been bogged down in the Senate and House of Representatives for weeks.

The current session of Congress is scheduled to end no later than Dec. 18. Lawmakers will remain on holiday until shortly after March 1, when U.S. President Bill Clinton's administration could impose sanctions on Colombia as part of its annual drug certification process.

The United States has threatened Colombia with the possibility of measures that would hurt the economy since last March when Washington -- citing President Ernesto Samper's alleged ties to drug lords -- effectively made Colombia a pariah state by including it on a list of countries that have failed to co-operate in the global anti-drug fight.

Michael Skol, a veteran U.S. diplomat who stepped down as deputy assistant secretary of state for Latin America earlier this year, told Reuters that laws mandating stiffer prison sentences for drug traffickers and so-called asset forfeiture were among the demands that Washington had made of Colombia in the wake of its decertification.
